article.title: Renewable Energy Feature
article.deck: How the quiet fields of Louisville, Illinois, became a powerhouse for the state's clean energy future.
article.body:
In the heart of Clay County, the landscape is shifting. Historically known for its rich soil and agricultural prowess, Louisville is now home to some of the most significant solar initiatives in Illinois. The introduction of the Maple Flats Solar Project has transformed 7,000 acres of rural land into a high-tech energy hub.

This transition isn't just about environmental impact; it's a massive economic engine. By repurposing land for photovoltaic arrays, the community is securing a legacy of energy leadership. Local residents are seeing the benefits through programs like Nexamp’s Community Solar, which allows families to save on electric costs without installing their own panels.

While the Little Wabash River once powered the town's early industry, it is now the Illinois sky that provides the next great resource, proving that small towns can lead the charge in a global energy revolution. The synergy between heritage and high-tech is defining the new Louisville.
article.alt:
## Image Alt Description

* **Aerial View:** An elevated drone shot capturing a solar farm installation situated amidst rural farmlands near Louisville, Illinois.
* **Layout:** Long, parallel rows of dark photovoltaic solar panels neatly arranged across a cleared plot of land.
* **Surrounding Landscape:** Expansive green agricultural fields, pastures, and patches of mature trees extending out to the horizon under a bright daytime sky.

history.title: Clay County Formation
history.description: Clay County was formed in 1824 out of portions of Wayne, Crawford, and Fayette counties. Its name is in honor of Henry Clay – famous American statesman, member of the United States Senate from Kentucky, and United States Secretary of State in the 19th Century. Clay was a candidate for President in the year the county was named. John Quincy Adams won however, and was elected President on February 9, 1825.
history.alt:

* **Environment:** Open public grounds surrounding the county seat's central architectural landmark under an overcast sky.

history.description: The A. F. & A. M. fraternity has a number of adherents in and about Louisville. They had a charter granted October 6, 1856. The following were charter members: S. C. Sparks, W. J. Stevenson, Wyatt Cook, Isaac Martin, J. A. Appersen, William McCracken and John Wooden. The lodge was named Louisville Lodge, No. 196. First officers were S. C. Sparks, Master; W. J. Stevenson, Senior Warden; Wyatt Cook, Junior Warden. Present officers: W. R. Whitman, Master; John Erwin, S.W.; G. A. Henry, J. W.; E. H. Hawkins, Treas.; G. W. Mills, Sec. ; John W. Sullivan, S. D.; G. K. Johnson, J. D.; B. F. Surrells, Tiler. The present membership is about forty. Their meetings are held in J. C. McCollum's Hall on Thursday night on or before each full moon. It is the oldest lodge in the county. Its present financial condition is good.

point_of_interest.landmark_description: The Flora Public Library is located in Library Park at 216 North Main Street. The 9,285 square foot facility was completed in 1992 and dedicated in March 1993. This spacious, modern building replaced the Flora Carnegie Library building, a two-story yellow brick, which stood in Library Park from 1903 until 1990. In January 1990, the Carnegie building was deemed structurally unsafe and closed to the public. After a two-year building campaign, along with the generosity and assistance of a supportive community, the new red brick structure was completed. https://florail.govoffice2.com/library

article.title: Community & Growth
article.body: As for Clay City, it continued to thrive during the boom years before and during World War I. The 1915 Pierce County Atlas lists Clay City with a population of 150. The Seattle Times reported that the factory employed 100 workmen at the kilns at its peak. Starting in 1916, the Eatonville Dispatch newspaper regularly included a neighborhood section with accounts of happenings in Clay City.

point_of_interest.landmark_description: Tacoma Eastern Railroad Company continued to expand its line from Tacoma toward Ashford, a starting point for expeditions to Mount Rainier. Far West Timber Company had a contract for clearing ahead of the tracks, and around 1902, loggers noticed massive deposits of clay when they uprooted trees about two miles south of Lake Kapowsin. The timber company negotiated with the railroad to purchase 320 acres of clay-laden land and then formed the Far West Clay Company. Within a short time, it became “the largest exclusive fire proofing plant in the Pacific Northwest,” according to a May 11, 1911, article in “The Clay Worker.”
point_of_interest.about_text: The clay was dumped from a 20-foot high trestle inside an enormous drying shed capable of holding 6,000 tons of clay. Machinery accelerated the drying process until the fire-proofing, as the prepared clay was called, advanced in its final form for ‘burning’ in large kilns. Bricks and other materials manufactured at this site could withstand high temperatures, a mark of the product’s strength and quality. The kilns, seven in all, were an unusual dome-shaped brick structure several feet tall. The machinery used to run the dryers and heat the kilns operated on steam power.

article.title: Healthy Water
article.body: An interesting story is one told of Sailor Springs. This village of a few hundred people is five and a half miles north of Clay City. In an early day there was found at this place a number of  springs with very peculiar water. This water was thought to be the cause of "milk-sick" and so the stock was fenced from the springs. In 1869 Mrs. Thomas M. Sailor of Ohio bought the land - four hundred acres - containing the springs. Mr. Sailor had the water tested and found it contained health-giving properties. Illuminating gas has been gathered from the springs and it has been thought it could be made of real value about the hotels. Back in the 70's and 80's the springs were liberally patronized as a summer resort. Two big hotels with fifty rooms each were often crowded while scores and perhaps hundreds lived in tents upon the beautiful grounds. In recent years the reputation of the springs has somewhat declined and the place is not so popular. https://clay.illinoisgenweb.org/hist1912soil.htm

article.title: The Tale of "Two Towns"
article.body: The village was laid out in 1834 along the old State Road. The founders chose the name "Xenia" (pronounced ZEE-nee-ə), a Greek word representing the ritualized laws of guest-friendship and hospitality. Historically, it implied a cultural duty to welcome travelers, provide them with food and shelter, and ensure safety without asking questions first.

* **Vehicles & Parking:** Several cars parked parallel along the asphalt street in front of the storefronts under an overcast sky.

point_of_interest.header1: U.S. National Register of Historic Places
point_of_interest.landmark_description: The Paine House is a historic house in Xenia, Illinois, which was the home of author Albert Bigelow Paine. Built in 1858, the house was designed using elements of the Greek Revival and Gothic Revival styles. Paine lived there from 1873 to 1888, during which he began his writing career, authoring numerous stories and poems. Several of his works appeared in Xenia's newspapers, inspiring his pursuit of a literary career. Paine later became known for his friendship with Mark Twain; he edited Twain's letters and wrote a multi-volume biography of the author. As of the 1980s, the house was still owned by Paine's descendants.
